title: Social commerce in China: how it works for US brands
summary: How social commerce in China works across Douyin, Xiaohongshu, Tmall and WeChat, and the 2026 livestream rules US brands need to plan for.
body_markdown:
In the US, content usually sends people to a shelf: an Amazon listing, a retailer, your own site. On[China's social platforms](https://www.pattern.com/blog/tackling-china--the-worlds-most-lucrative-ecommerce-market) , the content is the shelf. The same video or livestream finds the shopper, persuades them and takes the order, and the platform's algorithm decides who gets to see it.


That doesn't mean the shelf disappears. China runs on both: content that creates demand, and a shelf, usually a[Tmall or JD flagship store](https://www.pattern.com/blog/how-tmall-flagship-stores-recruit-and-retain-shoppers) , where much of that demand ends up buying. The job is to plan them together.


It also changes your risk. In February 2026, China began regulating livestream selling under a dedicated set of rules, and those rules reach brands as well as hosts.


Three things to know before you start:


1. **It's big, and it's mainstream.** Livestream ecommerce GMV exceeded RMB 5 trillion in 2025, close to a third of online retail, with an estimated 660 million users \[1\]\[2\].
2. **Each platform does a different job.** Tmall and JD are where people search. Douyin shows products to people who weren't looking. Xiaohongshu is where people go to research before they buy. WeChat is where the relationship continues. Planning one playbook for all of them is the most common mistake \[3\]\[4\]\[5\].
3. **The rules changed in 2026.** Livestream rooms now carry duties to verify sellers, review what is said before it goes live, keep records, and label AI-generated hosts \[6\]. For supplements, regulators are also targeting false health claims online \[7\].


## How Chinese shoppers actually buy


A white paper from the market regulator's research center and the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences describes the shift in plain terms: consumption is moving from "need, search, buy" toward "interest, scene, instant purchase" \[2\]. To succeed, US brands need to understand the role each platform plays in the consumer journey:


- **Interest ecommerce (**[Douyin](https://www.pattern.com/blog/what-is-douyin) **):** This is the growth accelerator. Through short videos and livestreaming, Douyin compresses the funnel from "seeing" to "buying" into seconds. The algorithm shows a product to people based on predicted interest, not only to an account's followers, so even a small account can sell in volume \[4\]. Content is built to trigger action: quick demonstrations, emotional hooks, live selling \[8\].
- **Social seeding (**[Xiaohongshu](https://www.pattern.com/blog/little-red-book-understanding-social-commerce-in-china) **):** This is where brand desirability and trust are born \[8\]. With more than 300 million monthly users \[5\], Xiaohongshu is the national decision gateway \[3\]. Chinese consumers are discerning and look for validation from peers over brand ads. Authentic user-generated content and micro-influencer reviews do the work here \[4\].
- **Shelf ecommerce (Tmall Global / JD Worldwide):** These platforms are where shoppers search and pay, which makes them the trust anchors and conversion hubs \[3\]. Once a brand is discovered on social platforms, Tmall or JD is the official flagship store where the purchase happens \[5\].
- **Private traffic (WeChat):** WeChat is the reservoir where brands retain customers, drive repeat purchases, run targeted marketing and build a deeper connection with them. By moving public traffic into Official Accounts and Mini Programs, brands can sidestep rising acquisition costs and focus on customer lifetime value (LTV) \[5\].


Search hasn't disappeared. It has moved inside the platforms. Xiaohongshu behaves like a search engine \[4\], and Douyin users search for what they see in the feed \[9\]. Shoppers also use outside search after discovery to confirm official details such as brand ownership, price consistency and authorized distribution \[9\]. If your prices or authorization are inconsistent, that is where it shows.


## Creators: who does what


[Creators fall into rough tiers](https://www.pattern.com/blog/5-steps-to-creating-a-successful-kol-marketing-campaign-us) , and each does a different job. In our experience, celebrities and top creators bring reach and credibility, mid-tier and tail creators do most of the converting, and KOCs (key opinion consumers) seed content that reads as real experience. Creator commissions on Douyin are high enough that they belong in your unit economics from the first day.


For supplements, substance beats slogans. Chinese supplement buyers research before they spend, and in our experience they respond to content that explains what's in the product, what the science says, and how it compares with the alternatives, delivered by someone credible. Educational content matters even more for supplements than for other categories. US supplement brand[Thorne increased its daily sales by 27% with regular three-hour livestreams on its Tmall store](https://www.pattern.com/blog/keys-to-ecommerce-growth-in-china-pattern-success-stories-and-best-practices) .


## Localize the value as well as the language


A name that's well known abroad is no longer enough. What resonates in China is relevance, and direct translations of global creative often fall flat. Localize the emotion, the humor and the tone of voice, and speak to a problem the Chinese shopper actually has. A skincare brand, for example, gets further by addressing the realities of long working days than by talking about its European heritage.


Take care with the benefit you promise. "Helps you recover after late nights" is a function claim. For supplements, lines like that can cross into territory the rules restrict \[6\]\[10\]. Localize the story, then[check the claim with counsel](https://www.pattern.com/blog/china-market-entry-list) before it goes into a script.


## Put the economics on one page


Before you commit, build a P&L for each platform that includes:


- creator commissions and agency fees
- paid traffic
- platform fees
- returns
- the price you can hold across platforms


Brands that model social commerce on US influencer economics tend to underestimate this. Treat the content as the sales channel, with channel costs to match.


## China's 2026 livestream ecommerce rules


The core of the 2026 rules is aimed at one format:[livestream selling](https://www.pattern.com/blog/what-western-brands-can-learn-from-livestreaming-in-china) . China's first national rules for it, the Measures for the Supervision and Administration of Livestream E-commerce, took effect on February 1, 2026. SAMR (the market regulator) and CAC (the internet regulator) issued them on December 18, 2025 \[6\]. They put duties on four parties:


- **Platforms** that host livestream selling, such as Douyin.
- **Room operators:** whoever runs a livestream room and sells through it. That can be your own brand account, or a creator or agency running a room for you.
- **Hosts:** the people on camera.
- **Agencies** that manage hosts, often called MCNs.


For brands, five duties matter most \[6\]:


- **Know who is selling.** Platforms verify room operators, re-checking at least every six months, and hosts' real identities. Operators check the licences and product certificates of the business actually selling the goods.
- **Review before you go live.** Operators vet what will be shown and said in advance, and correct misstatements on air, with a record.
- **Don't mislead.** No false or misleading claims about function, quality, sales, reviews or credentials, including AI-fabricated ones. Any discount must show the price it is calculated from.
- **Label AI hosts.** AI-generated people must be labelled for the whole stream.
- **Keep the records.** Transaction data, replays and interaction records must be kept for at least three years.


Supplements get extra attention. For supplements sold cross-border, the safe position is no health-function claims at all \[10\]. In general trade, a draft SAMR measure published in May 2026 would tie health-food advertising to the claims in the product's registration certificate or filing, rule out disease-prevention and treatment claims, and tighten supervision of livestream advertising \[11\]\[12\]. It's a draft, and its final text may differ.


## Before you launch: a China social commerce checklist


- Decided what the content must do on each platform: discover, persuade, convert or retain
- Localized the story, and checked every benefit claim with counsel before it goes into a script
- Wrote an approved-claims list per product, with legal review before it goes to creators
- Set up pre-stream review, on-air correction and record-keeping, and agreed in writing who does each
- Verified every creator and agency, with written agreements covering content and product quality
- Settled price discipline and authorized sellers before scaling content spend
- Planned paid support behind content that has already earned attention
- Built a P&L per platform that includes commissions, paid traffic, platform fees and returns
- Set a price corridor and checked that discount baselines are shown
- Planned how to bring buyers into WeChat so they come back
- Agreed what data and replays you will receive, and how often
- Marked the next sales peak,[618](https://www.pattern.com/blog/from-discounts-to-decisions-what-6-18-tells-us-about-chinas-next-ecommerce-chapter) or[Double 11](https://www.pattern.com/blog/what-every-global-brand-should-know-about-11-11-in-china) , and worked back from it


## Planning social commerce in China with Pattern


Social commerce in China is a different way of shopping, built on peer-led discovery and community. The plumbing for foreign brands is largely in place:[cross-border platforms](https://www.pattern.com/blog/cross-border-ecommerce-asia-benefits-challenges) let you hold stock in bonded warehouses in China or ship from overseas \[13\]. What's often missing is a local partner who can bridge the cultural gap, work with authentic voices, and now also run the compliance process the 2026 rules require. In China, trust is earned through content, and the brands that adapt early will be best positioned to benefit.


Pattern helps brands plan social commerce in China alongside the shelf, with[China Accelerator](https://www.pattern.com/marketplace/china-accelerator) , local teams in Shanghai, Guangzhou, Shenzhen and Hong Kong, and as a Gold Trading Partner on Tmall Global.[Talk to our China team](https://www.pattern.com/contact/china) .


## Frequently asked questions


### What is social commerce in China?


It's shopping where the content does the selling. A short video or livestream on a platform like Douyin finds the shopper, persuades them and takes the order. Livestream ecommerce alone passed RMB 5 trillion in GMV in 2025, close to a third of China's online retail \[1\]\[2\].


### What is the difference between Douyin and Xiaohongshu?


Douyin shows products to people based on predicted interest, so it's built for discovery and fast conversion \[4\]\[8\]. Xiaohongshu is where shoppers research and read peer reviews before they buy, so it's where trust and desirability are built \[3\]\[8\].


### What are China's 2026 livestream ecommerce rules?


The Measures for the Supervision and Administration of Livestream E-commerce took effect on February 1, 2026. They require platforms and room operators to verify who is selling, review content before going live, avoid misleading claims, label AI-generated hosts and keep records for at least three years \[6\].


### Can supplement brands make health claims in Chinese livestreams?


For supplements sold cross-border, the safe position is no health-function claims at all \[10\]. In general trade, a May 2026 draft SAMR measure would tie health-food advertising to the claims in the product's registration certificate or filing \[11\]\[12\].
